title: Quantum Complexity in Nuclear Scattering and Fission Dynamics
authors: Saurabh V. Kadam, Antonio Bjelčić, Nicolas Schunck, Kyle Wendt
abstract: Quantum computers promise advantages for simulating strongly correlated quantum many-body systems, like atomic nuclei, that are beyond the reach of classical computers. Realizing this potential requires understanding the quantum complexity structure of the target problem. We investigate the time-evolution of two key indicators of quantum complexity, bipartite entanglement entropy and non-local magic (non-stabilizerness), in nuclear reaction dynamics. We analyze two representative dynamical processes: scattering in a one-dimensional model of strongly interacting fermions governed by the Negele potential, and a realistic simulation of $^{240}$Pu fission within time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (TDHFB) theory. In the former case, we find that interactions dynamically generate both entanglement and non-local magic, leaving persistent signatures of quantum complexity in the outgoing states. In the latter, we observe that substantial quantum complexity survives in the spatial bipartition of daughter fragments well beyond scission. The presence of significant non-local magic and entanglement in both cases strongly indicate that quantum computers would provide substantial advantages for accurately simulating nuclear reaction dynamics.
summary: This work quantifies the quantum complexity of nuclear processes, such as scattering and fission, by tracking entanglement and non-local magic resources over time. By showing that these complexity measures remain high in the outgoing fragments, the authors argue that simulating these dynamics accurately requires quantum computation. This establishes a theoretical case for quantum advantage in nuclear structure physics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the quantum complexity structure of strongly correlated quantum many-body systems to determine if they are suitable candidates for quantum computational advantage.
main_result: The analysis of nuclear scattering and fission dynamics shows that significant quantum complexity, quantified by entanglement and non-local magic, persists in the outgoing states, suggesting quantum computers would offer substantial advantages.
method: The study analyzes the time-evolution of quantum complexity indicators, specifically bipartite entanglement entropy and non-local magic, using theoretical frameworks like the stabilizer formalism and Gaussian state approximations.
model_or_system: The models include a one-dimensional system of strongly interacting fermions governed by the Negele potential for scattering, and a realistic simulation of $^{240}	ext{Pu}$ fission using time-dependent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov (TDHFB) theory.
key_observables: Bipartite entanglement entropy, non-local magic (non-stabilizerness), and the Anti-flatness ($	ext{F}_A$) measure.
important_parameters: The complexity measures are sensitive to the dynamics, particularly in the region beyond scission during fission.
main_assumptions: The analysis uses Gaussian states (FGS) as a tractable proxy for the full dynamical evolution, despite FGSs being classically simulable.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by defining and analyzing quantum complexity measures (entanglement, non-local magic) and applying these tools to two distinct physical scenarios: 1D fermion scattering and $^{240}	ext{Pu}$ fission dynamics.
why_interesting: It bridges the gap between abstract quantum information theory (complexity measures) and concrete, complex physical systems (nuclear reactions), providing a theoretical benchmark for quantum simulation feasibility in nuclear physics.
